AbstractText.Label: UNLABELLED
AbstractText.content: It is still unclear if an isoenergetic, sucrose-rich diet leads to health consequences.

AbstractText.Label: AIMS
AbstractText.content: To investigate the effects of excessive sucrose within an isoenergetic diet on metabolic parameters in male C57BL/6 mice.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Animals were fed a control diet (10% fat, 8% sucrose - SC group), a high-sucrose diet (10% fat, 32% sucrose - HSu group), a high-fat diet (42% fat, 8% sucrose - HF group) or a high-fat/high-sucrose diet (42% fat, 32% sucrose - HF/HSu group) for 8 weeks.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Mice fed HF and HF/HSu diets gained more body mass (BM) and more body adiposity than SC- or Hsu-fed mice. Despite the unchanged BM and adiposity indices, HSu mice presented adipocyte hypertrophy, which was also observed in the HF and HF/HSu groups (P<.0001). The HF, HSu and HF/HSu mice were glucose intolerant and had elevated serum insulin levels (P<.05). The levels of leptin, resistin and monocyte chemotactic protein-1 increased, while the serum adiponectin decreased in the HF, HSu and HF/HSu groups (P<.05). In the adipose tissue, the HF, HSu and HF/HSu groups showed higher levels of leptin expression and lower levels of adiponectin expression in comparison with the SC group (P<.05). Liver steatosis was higher in the HF, HSu and HF/HSu groups than in the SC group (P<.0001). Hepatic cholesterol was higher in the HF and HF/HSu groups, while hepatic TG was higher in the HSu and HF/HSu groups (P<.05). In hepatic tissue, the sterol receptor element-binding protein-1c expression was increased in the HF, HSu and HF/HSu groups, unlike the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha expression that decreased in the HF, HSu and HF/HSu groups in comparison with the SC group (P<.05).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: A sucrose-rich diet does not lead to a state of obesity but has the potential to cause changes in the adipocytes (hypertrophy) as well as glucose intolerance, hyperinsulinemia, hyperlipidemia, hepatic steatosis and increases in the number of inflammatory cytokines. The deleterious effects of a sucrose-rich diet in an animal model, even when the sucrose replaces starch isocalorically in the feed, can have far-reaching consequences for health.
